body:
OBJECTIVES
- Students explain how the environments of the Sahara, Sahel and savanna shaped what each region produced and traded (D2.Geo.11.6-8).
- Students explain how the decisions of rulers and traders affected the well-being of people and kingdoms (D2.Eco.1.6-8).
- Students analyze how the perspectives of outside writers shaped the sources they created, and detect limits in the historical record, including the role of oral tradition (D2.His.6.6-8, D2.His.10.6-8, RH.6-8.6).
- Students cite specific evidence from primary sources (RH.6-8.1).
- Students evaluate the relative influence of several causes of Mali's power and support a claim with logical reasoning and accurate evidence (D2.His.15.6-8, D2.His.16.6-8, WHST.6-8.1.B).

MATERIALS
- Gold, Salt and the Sahara (lesson reading)
- Two Writers Describe Mali (primary sources, adapted and paraphrased)
- A physical map of North and West Africa showing the Sahara, Sahel, Niger River, Taghaza, Timbuktu, Gao and Cairo
- A short recorded or read-aloud passage from the Sundiata epic (in a published school edition, if your library has one)
- A source comparison chart: author, from where, when, how they knew, what they noticed, what they might miss

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read the overview. Map the vegetation zones and trade routes. Quick write: if you lived where there was gold but no salt, what would you do? Begin the lesson, Gold, Salt and the Sahara.
Day 2: Finish the lesson. Introduce griots and oral tradition by reading aloud a short passage from the Sundiata epic; discuss how memory and performance preserve history.
Day 3: Students work through Mali Through Travelers' Eyes, filling in the source comparison chart for al-Umari and Ibn Battuta.
Day 4: Students write their claims. Whole-class discussion: what voices are missing from these sources (farmers, miners, women, enslaved people, the people of Mali themselves)?
Day 5: Assessment: What Made Mali Powerful?

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: provide a cause-and-effect chain for the gold-salt trade (environment, need, trade, taxes, power) with blanks to complete. Pre-teach mansa, caravan and pilgrimage.
- Support: highlight one key sentence in each source and offer the frame "This source was written by ___, who was from ___. Because of that, ___."
- Stretch: look at the Catalan Atlas of 1375, which shows Mansa Musa holding a gold nugget, and explain what it shows about how Europeans saw Mali.
- Multilingual learners: use a picture glossary of camel caravan, salt slab and gold dust; allow partners to talk through the source comparison chart in their home language first; give a word bank for the argument (because, as a result, however, most important).

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
We are studying the great empires of West Africa: Ghana, Mali and Songhai. Your child will learn how gold and salt were traded across the Sahara Desert, about Mansa Musa's famous journey to Mecca in 1324, and about the scholars and libraries of Timbuktu. We will also learn about griots, the oral historians who kept history alive through storytelling. Ask your child: why would someone trade gold for salt? You might also share a story your family has passed down by word of mouth.
title: Teacher guide: West African Empires
